subject: physics_2
question_text: Explain the formation of stationary waves in stretched strings and hence deduce the laws of transverse waves in stretched strings.

verification.note: The 1+2+1+2+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it — the figure carries 0 marks because the question does not ask for a diagram. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: y₁ + y₂ = A sin(kx − ωt) + A sin(kx + ωt) = 2A sin kx cos ωt (sum-to-product identity); nodes where sin kx = 0, antinodes where sin kx = ±1; p loops in length l give λ = 2l/p; with v = √(T/μ) the frequency is n = (p/2l)√(T/μ), and the three laws read off from the fundamental n = (1/2l)√(T/μ).

recall_prompt: Say the derivation in order — the two waves, the resultant, nodes and antinodes, the frequency formula, and the three laws.

steps.label: Stationary wave and its formation
lines: Stationary wave: when two progressive
waves of the same amplitude and
frequency, travelling along the same
line in opposite directions, superpose,
a stationary wave is formed.
A string fixed between two rigid
supports is plucked. The transverse
waves travel to the supports, reflect
there, and superpose with the incident
waves on the string.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Same amplitude, same frequency, opposite directions — all three conditions in one sentence.
steps.why: The three conditions are what make the pattern stand still: equal and opposite wave motions cancel the travelling part and leave a vibration fixed in place. The rigid supports supply the oppositely moving wave by reflection.
common_mistakes: Leaving out same amplitude — unequal amplitudes leave a partly travelling wave.
Saying the stationary wave travels along the string — the pattern stays in place; only the particles vibrate.

recall.must_convey: That two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose, the reflected wave supplying the opposite direction.
accept: same amplitude and frequency, opposite directions
reject: Y equals 2A sin kx cos omega t

steps.memory_tip: Three sames — amplitude, frequency, line — and one opposite: direction.

steps.label: String vibrating in loops
steps.margin_note: The string between supports P and Q, vibrating in loops — a node at each support, an antinode mid-loop.
steps.why: The figure fixes the counting the derivation uses: the fixed ends are nodes, each loop is half a wavelength, and p loops fill the length l.
common_mistakes: Drawing an antinode at a fixed support — a fixed end cannot move, so it is always a node.

recall.must_convey: That the string vibrates in loops between the supports, with nodes at the fixed ends.
accept: draw the string with loops between P and Q
mark a node and an antinode
reject: p loops give lambda equals 2l by p

steps.memory_tip: Fixed ends are always nodes — start the sketch there and the loops draw themselves.

steps.label: Superposition and resultant wave
steps.mark_note: Y = 2A sin kx cos ωt derived
lines: Let the incident and reflected waves be:

lines.text: y₁ = A sin(kx − ωt) , y₂ = A sin(kx + ωt)

lines: By the principle of superposition:

lines.text: Y = A sin(kx − ωt) + A sin(kx + ωt)
Using sin(C−D) + sin(C+D) = 2 sin C cos D:

lines: This is the stationary wave. A particle
at position x vibrates with amplitude
2A sin kx.
steps.margin_note: Two marks: writing the two waves, and reaching Y = 2A sin kx cos ωt through the identity.
steps.why: The identity separates position from time: sin kx fixes how MUCH each point vibrates and cos ωt says WHEN — and a product of the two, with no (kx − ωt) argument left, is exactly what a wave that does not travel looks like.
common_mistakes: Writing both waves with the same sign of ωt — the reflected wave travels the opposite way, so the signs must differ.
Losing the factor 2 in the sum-to-product identity.
Reading 2A sin kx as a displacement — it is the AMPLITUDE at position x; the displacement still oscillates as cos ωt.

recall.must_convey: That adding A sin(kx − ωt) and A sin(kx + ωt) gives Y = 2A sin kx cos ωt.
accept: add the incident and reflected waves
reject: nodes where sin kx is zero

steps.memory_tip: Opposite signs of ωt go in; position and time come out separated — sin kx times cos ωt.

steps.label: Nodes and antinodes
lines: The amplitude 2A sin kx is zero where
sin kx = 0:
and maximum where sin kx = ±1:
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both position lists, read directly from 2A sin kx.
steps.why: The node and antinode positions are not new facts — they fall out of the amplitude factor sin kx, which is why deriving Y first makes this step one line of reading.
common_mistakes: Spacing nodes λ apart — consecutive zeros of sin kx sit λ/2 apart.
Swapping the two lists — x = 0 is a node (the fixed end), not an antinode.

recall.must_convey: That nodes sit at x = 0, λ/2, λ … and antinodes at λ/4, 3λ/4 …, from the amplitude 2A sin kx.
accept: nodes where sin kx is zero
antinodes where sin kx is plus or minus one
x equals lambda by four for the first antinode

steps.memory_tip: Read the amplitude factor: zeros of sin kx are nodes, peaks are antinodes.

steps.label: Frequency of vibration
lines: A string of length l fixed at both ends
vibrates in p loops. Each loop is half a
wavelength long:
The speed of a transverse wave on the
string, with tension T and linear
density μ:
So the frequency of vibration:
steps.margin_note: Two marks: λ = 2l/p from the loop count, then n = v/λ with v = √(T/μ).
steps.why: Both ends are nodes, so a whole number of half-wavelength loops must fit the length exactly — that boundary condition is what turns the continuous formula v = nλ into a formula with the loop count p in it.
common_mistakes: Writing λ = l/p — each loop is λ/2, not λ, so λ = 2l/p.
Using mass instead of linear density in v = √(T/μ) — μ is mass PER UNIT LENGTH.

recall.must_convey: That p half-wavelength loops fit the length l, and n = v/λ gives (p/2l)√(T/μ).
accept: p loops of lambda by two fill the string
n equals p by 2l root T by mu
reject: n is inversely proportional to the length

steps.memory_tip: Loops are half-waves: p halves fill l, so λ = 2l/p — the rest is v = nλ.

steps.label: The three laws
lines: With p = 1, the fundamental frequency is
From this equation the laws of
transverse waves follow:
I law: the fundamental frequency is
inversely proportional to the length.
II law: it is directly proportional to
the square root of the tension.
III law: it is inversely proportional to
the square root of the linear density.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Each law needs its statement AND its constant pair in brackets.
steps.why: Each law is the fundamental formula read with two of the three quantities held constant — stating which two are constant is what makes each proportionality a law rather than a fragment.
common_mistakes: Dropping the square roots in laws II and III — n varies as √T and 1/√μ, never as T or 1/μ.
Leaving out the constant quantities — n ∝ 1/l is only true with T and μ fixed.
Stating the laws for an overtone — the laws are written for the fundamental, p = 1.

recall.must_convey: That n ∝ 1/l, n ∝ √T and n ∝ 1/√μ, each with the other two quantities constant.
accept: inversely proportional to root linear density

steps.memory_tip: One formula, three readings: l plain and inverted, T and μ under square roots.

insider_note: The laws at the end are read off n = (1/2l)√(T/μ) — derive the formula carefully and the last two marks are a reading exercise, not new work.
